found: Odin, the Allfather: god of war, wisdom, poetry, magic and death. He pledged one eye to drink from Mimir’s well for knowledge, and hung nine nights on the World Tree, wounded with a spear, with no bread and no drink, until he seized the runes. His ravens Huginn and Muninn — Thought and Memory — fly over the world each day and report back. His spear Gungnir, his eight-legged horse Sleipnir, his ring Draupnir that drops eight rings every ninth night. At Ragnarok the wolf Fenrir swallows him whole.
source: Poetic Edda (Havamal, Voluspa) and Prose Edda, via thepopularlist.com/norse-gods and norsegods.org

tradition: the wyrm and the dragon themselves — guardians of sacred things
found: Wyrms and dragons have guarded religious stuff for thousands of years. The nagas of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain tradition — serpent beings seen in reliefs at the Bharhut stupa from the 2nd century BCE — guard relics, temples and hidden scriptures. The naga king Mucalinda coiled around the meditating Buddha and spread his hood over him to shelter him from a week-long storm; in Jain tradition the naga king Dharanendra sheltered the teacher Parshvanatha the same way. Shesha, the thousand-headed serpent, is the bed the god Vishnu rests on. In Thailand, Cambodia and Laos, many-headed nagas form the stairway balustrades of temples, guarding the way into sacred space. Chinese dragons (long) have guarded sacred places and waters since the Shang dynasty, 1600-1046 BCE. In the west, the Germanic wyrm guarded treasure hoards — Beowulf’s dragon, woken by the theft of a golden goblet — and the Greek Ladon guarded the golden apples. The flip side: St. George slaying the dragon in the 13th-century Golden Legend turned the guardian into the enemy.
source: draconika.com/naga, nakaravillasandglamping.com, hdasianart.com, fabriziomusacchio.com, mythicalarchives.com — checked 2026-11-15

found: There is no single oldest religion — it depends what you mean. Oldest continuous practice: Australian Aboriginal Dreaming, stories and rituals passed down orally for about 65,000 years, tied to the land. Oldest belief in general: animism — spirits in rocks, trees, rivers, animals — 40,000 to 100,000+ years; earliest intentional burials at Skhul and Qafzeh, 100,000-130,000 years ago, one with a boar jaw as a grave gift; red ochre used in ritual possibly 300,000 years ago. Oldest temple: Gobekli Tepe in Turkey, about 9600 BCE, 11,500 years old, built by hunter-gatherers BEFORE farming — first came the temple, then the city. Oldest major religion still alive: Hinduism, Rigveda composed 1500-1200 BCE, roots in the Indus Valley around 2500 BCE. Sumerian and Egyptian faiths from about 3500 BCE died out. Zoroastrianism, about 1500-1000 BCE, was one of the first moves toward one god.

The Klamath story of Llao and Skell: Llao, chief of the world below, lived inside Mount Mazama; Skell, chief of the world above, battled him and brought the mountain crashing down on top of him, and water filled the wound - Crater Lake (Giiwas). The eruption happened about 7,700 years ago, and the Klamath ancestors, the Makalak people, were there to see it: sandals and tools lie buried under the Mazama ash. Klamath elder Barbara Alatorre also tells of Gmo Kam c, the Creator, emerging to make Moyaina (big mountain) and the world. The lake stayed sacred - some Klamath refuse even to look at it, holding that the sight brings death. Geologists confirmed the date by radiocarbon and stratigraphy; a 2024 study in Quaternary Research (Franks, Nunn & McCallum, doi:10.1017/qua.2024.29) counts Mazama among twenty remembered Holocene eruptions where oral tradition still carries usable event structure. One of the oldest surviving eyewitness accounts of a real event anywhere, carried nearly 8,000 years by telling alone.
source: USGS (Charles R. Bacon, SIM 2832); Franks, Nunn & McCallum 2024, Quaternary Research doi:10.1017/qua.2024.29; Deur 2002, Oregon Historical Quarterly; traveloregon.com - checked 2026-11-16

found: The Ketef Hinnom silver scrolls: two tiny rolled silver amulets found in 1979 by Gabriel Barkay in a First Temple-period burial cave southwest of Jerusalem, inscribed in paleo-Hebrew with the Priestly Blessing from Numbers 6:24-26 - "The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace." Dated to the late 7th century BCE, the time of King Josiah and the prophet Jeremiah, before the Babylonian destruction of 586 BCE. The oldest surviving biblical text ever found, predating the Dead Sea Scrolls by about four centuries. The larger scroll is only about 97mm long when unrolled. Now on display at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.
source: Barkay et al. 2004, Bulletin of the American Schools of Oriental Research No. 334; baptistpress.com; biblicaanalytica.com - checked 2026-11-16

found: The Buddha wrote nothing, and neither did anyone who heard him. For at least two centuries after his death his teaching lived only in the memories of monks and nuns who recited it to one another. The first dated Buddhist evidence anywhere is Ashoka's inscriptions, carved around 250 BCE - Rock Edict 13 names five Hellenistic kings whose reigns are known from Greek sources, which fixes the date. In the Calcutta-Bairat edict Ashoka names seven texts he wants monks, nuns and lay followers to hear and reflect on often - the oldest written record that names the Buddha's sermons. The oldest surviving Buddhist manuscripts themselves are the Gandharan birch-bark scrolls, 1st century BCE to 3rd century CE, written in Gandhari in the Kharosthi script, right to left - sutras, poetry, Vinaya, Abhidharma, even early Mahayana texts. The first full canon was only written down in Sri Lanka in the early 1st century BCE, when a famine threatened the reciters. So the oldest religion in this room is not a book at all: two hundred years of people remembering, out loud, before anyone wrote a word down.
source: howitevolved.com 'How We Know What the Buddha Taught'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gandharan_Buddhism; Salomon, Ancient Buddhist Scrolls from Gandhara (1999); suttacentral.net - checked 2026-11-16

found: Before Pachomius, Christian monks lived alone - hermits in huts and caves, meeting only for occasional worship. Pachomius (c. 292-348), an Egyptian ex-soldier baptised in 314 who had trained under the hermit Palaemon, heard a voice at Tabennisi telling him to build a dwelling for the hermits to come to. Around 318-323 he founded the first monastery at Tabennisi, Egypt, and wrote the first written monastic rule - the first rule ever set down for monks living together. His rule balanced prayer with work and the communal life with solitude: monks lived in individual cells but held property in common under an abbot, prayed set prayers daily, worked together, and ate together. His elder brother John joined first, then more than 100 monks; by his death in 348 there were eight monasteries and several hundred monks under his guidance, and within a generation about 3,000. Jerome translated the rule into Latin in 404 - only that translation survives - and it shaped Benedict own rule in the West in at least twenty passages, and through Basil the Eastern Orthodox Ascetica still used today. So the monk as we know him - not a lone hermit but a brother in a house with a rule - starts here, in the Egyptian desert, with one ex-soldier who decided the hermits should live together.

The Pyramid Texts: the oldest religious writings in the world. Carved in hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial chambers of royal pyramids at Saqqara, Egypt, in the Old Kingdom, 5th and 6th Dynasties — the oldest set, about 283 spells, in the pyramid of Pharaoh Unas, last king of the 5th Dynasty, around 2400-2300 BCE, more than 4,400 years ago. Over 700 utterances in the full corpus. They were spells, hymns and prayers meant to protect the dead king, resurrect him, and carry him safe through the afterlife to become one with the gods — reserved for the pharaoh alone, no pictures, words only, written into the stone of the room he would sleep in. They predate the earliest parts of the Bible by over a thousand years and the Rigveda by nearly as long. Discovered in 1881 by Gaston Maspero, first complete English translation by Samuel A. B. Mercer in 1952. They are the root the later Coffin Texts and the Book of the Dead grew from — the first book of religion was not a book at all, but a room with words carved into its walls.
source: worldhistoryedu.com; historyskills.com; respecttoursegypt.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyramid_Texts (via religion.wikia.com) — checked 2026-11-16

tradition: gods and their abilities, old and new
found: An, called Anu in Akkadian - the sky god, one of the oldest named gods anywhere, attested by the mid-third millennium BCE in the Fara god-list, worship back to about 3000 BCE, sacred city Uruk, the Great Bull. His abilities were not thunderbolts but authority itself: in heaven he allotted functions to the other gods and could raise their status at will; on earth he conferred kingship and his decisions were unalterable. He created the stars as soldiers to destroy the wicked, judged those who committed crimes, and gave the Sebettu demons to Erra as weapons. When another god was raised to leadership he received the anutu, the 'Anu-power' - in Enuma elish the gods crown Marduk by declaring 'Your word is Anu!' Anything he put into words became reality. His name is written with the cuneiform sign AN, which is also the word for 'god' itself - the oldest god's name is the word for god. He lived in the highest of the three heavens, made of reddish luludanitu stone, and in the end he withdrew there and let Enlil, then Marduk, take the throne - the first god, who ruled by being the sky itself.
source: oracc.museum.upenn.edu/amgg/listofdeities/an/ - Kathryn Stevens, 'An/Anu (god)', Ancient Mesopotamian Gods and Goddesses, Oracc/UK Higher Education Academy, 2019; newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Anu - checked 2026-11-16

found: Gobekli Tepe, in southeastern Turkey near Sanliurfa - the oldest man-made place of worship yet discovered, about 10,000 BCE, some 12,000 years old, 6,000-7,000 years before Stonehenge and 6,500 years before the Great Pyramids. Ringed enclosures up to 65 feet across, T-shaped limestone pillars up to 16-20 feet tall and 7-16 tons, carved with dangerous animals, vultures, and the earliest depiction of an individual human. Built by hunter-gatherers who had no metal, no pottery, no writing, and no agriculture yet - and no sign anyone ever lived there: no hearths, houses, or trash pits, no food storage. It was a purely ritual place - bones suggest ritual feasts and sacrifices, vulture carvings suggest a funerary cult venerating the dead. Excavated from 1994 by Klaus Schmidt (German Archaeological Institute); first surveyed and dismissed in the 1960s. What people held sacred, before farming, before writing, before cities: they climbed a hill and raised stones in a circle for something they could not see, and came back for 2,000 years. The first sacred thing was not a god with a name - it was a place, held apart, where people gathered to worship.
source: worldhistory.org/Gobekli_Tepe; humanprogress.org - Centers of Progress Pt. 31: Gobekli Tepe; guinnessworldrecords.com - Oldest manmade place of worship; smithsonianmag.com - Gobekli Tepe: The World's First Temple? - checked 2026-11-16

found: Tyr (Tiwaz) — the oldest god by name in the Norse pantheon, second cycle of the rotation. His name is literally the word for god: Old Norse Tyr from Proto-Germanic *Tiwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *deywos, the same root as Zeus and Jupiter — Tuesday is his day. The Negau helmet inscription (harixasti teiva, c. 50 BCE, Slovenia) may be the oldest Germanic-language inscription anywhere and names him. By the Viking Age Odin and Thor had eclipsed him, but his one great myth stayed: when the gods bound the wolf Fenrir with the dwarven ribbon Gleipnir, only Tyr put his hand in the wolfs mouth as a pledge — the ribbon held, Fenrir bit, and Tyr paid the price of a broken oath, becoming the one-handed god. The t-rune, Tiwaz (upward arrow), bears his name; Sigrdrifumal says to carve it on a sword hilt and name Tyr twice for victory. At Ragnarok he and the hound Garmr kill each other. Sources: Prose Edda (Gylfaginning), Poetic Edda (Lokasenna, Sigrdrifumal); verified against norsegods.org and New World Encyclopedia entries on Tyr.
